summary:
Acre stands under Brazil's national framework, which applies in full within the state: same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since the National Justice Council resolution of 14 May 2013, carried 14-1, joint adoption has been available since 2010 with full rights from 2015, and the age of consent is equal regardless of sexual orientation.

Legal gender change has required no surgery, hormones or diagnosis since the Supreme Federal Court ruling of 1 March 2018, and the process proceeds by self-determination. National identity documents carry no third-gender option, but civil registries have accepted "non-binary/unspecified" entries since 2020 and a Superior Court of Justice ruling of 6 May 2025 permits neutral-gender registry rectification as precedent. A trans voter may register under lived name and identity even before documents are updated. A trans visitor's status and documents are handled on the same footing as anyone else's at entry and in family matters.

On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court held discrimination and violence on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity to be a crime equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989, punishable by imprisonment of one to five years and fines (ADO 26 and MI 4733). An expat legal guide updated in April 2026 confirms that same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules operate nationwide. Courts have applied the provisions to commercial conduct: the 27th Private Chamber of the São Paulo Court of Justice upheld a moral-damage award against a nightclub that refused entry to a trans woman wearing women's clothing.

Enforcement does not match the text. OutRight International's country report, last updated 12 March 2026, records that Brazil's LGBTIQ legal advances face repeal pressure in a conservative Congress and that the country retains one of the world's highest rates of violence against sexual and gender minorities, particularly trans people. The April 2026 expat guide describes major cities such as São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro and Brasília as broadly welcoming with established legal infrastructure, while smaller cities and rural areas, including those in Acre, may present more social friction despite identical legal rights.

Documented violence includes "boa noite, Cinderela" drink-spiking robberies in which LGBTQIA+ people were targeted in São Paulo nightlife, investigated in May 2024, and a climate of intimidation around the October 2024 municipal elections, where close to 1,000 transgender candidates stood across every state and received death threats; the number of trans officeholders tripled against the previous cycle, and over 3,000 openly LGBTQ candidates ran in the same election. The first transgender federal legislators, Salabert and Hilton, were elected in 2022.

Protection machinery has widened. An analysis of case law from 2022 records lower courts pressing the Superior Court of Justice toward unanimously extending the remedies of the Maria da Penha Law and the Feminicide Law to trans women, bringing trans people within the country's violence-prevention statutes.

Detention carries a specific and contested regime. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, governs where LGBTI people who are arrested or imprisoned are housed. A person is recognised as LGBTI for these purposes by self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing. On arrest the place of deprivation of liberty is fixed by a judge in a reasoned decision after the person has been consulted: the judge must set out available male, female and LGBTI-specific units and ask trans, travesti and intersex people whether they prefer custody in a female, male or specific unit, and within it the general population or a specific wing or cell. The declared preference is recorded, later change of placement is possible, transfers are prioritised where there is violence or a serious threat, LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited.

Practice does not reliably follow that framework. A peer-reviewed census of travestis and transgender women held in Rio de Janeiro state prisons between April and June 2021 interviewed 138 self-declared travesti and trans-woman inmates inside eleven units treated as masculine in the metropolitan region, and documents that in that system travestis and trans women are housed in units operated as masculine, with some held in so-called neutral or security units. The study treats placement in male units as a double punishment compounded by recurring violations of basic rights, and notes a 2015 Rio de Janeiro state law granting parity of treatment with cisgender women in women's units covering hair length, feminine clothing, accessories and cosmetics, alongside national norms from 2014 and 2020 that permit people to be housed where they choose, including in units denominated masculine.
tangentialFactors:
On paper Brazil's LGBTQ+ protections are among the most progressive in Latin America, yet the same inventory rates the country's violence against sexual and gender minorities as among the world's highest, concentrated on trans people. The gap between statutory protection and street-level outcome is the central turbulence a visitor should expect.

Legal advances are politically contested: an international rights organisation's March 2026 report describes repeal pressure in a conservative Congress, so the protective framework in force is contested rather than settled.

Local political visibility has risen sharply, with the first transgender federal legislators elected in 2022, over 3,000 openly LGBTQ candidates in the 2024 municipal election and trans officeholders tripling in number. Visibility and threat have moved together, since trans candidates in the same cycle received death threats and intimidation.

Geographic unevenness matters for an Acre itinerary: the available guidance contrasts large metropolitan centres with established legal infrastructure against smaller cities and rural areas, including those in Acre, where identical legal rights may coexist with greater social friction.

Commercial and nightlife settings are documented risk sites, from the upheld refusal-of-entry case against a nightclub to the drink-spiking robberies targeting LGBTQIA+ patrons in São Paulo nightlife in May 2024.

outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no Acre-specific enforcement record: no prosecution, incident, detention placement or state-level administrative decision within Acre is sourced here, so conditions inside the state rest on the national framework plus one guide's general contrast between major cities and smaller or rural areas.

No source in this inventory addresses trans-specific healthcare access, medication continuity or trans-serving facilities in Acre; that layer remains not sourced rather than confirmed absent.

Entry and screening practice for trans visitors is described only at the level of national rule, that documents and status are handled on the same footing as anyone else's; no Acre or Brazilian border-procedure account of how markers are read at the frontier is included, so front-line screening behaviour is unresolved.

The prison census cited is drawn from Rio de Janeiro state units between April and June 2021 and is the only empirical detention data available here; whether the mismatch it records also occurs in Acre's detention facilities is unresolved and not inferred.

Whether the National Council of Justice housing rules have been applied, contested or ignored in Acre's custody hearings is unresolved in this inventory, as is the current legislative status of the repeal pressure reported in March 2026.
